Welcome to the Winter Palace, Tsar Alexander. Your empire is vast and its burdens are old: the serfs wait for freedom, the provinces for self-government, the army for reform. Free your peasants, let the Zemstvos govern the land, and Russia will grow strong from within.
Alexander II
Emperor and Autocrat of All Russia, Tsar of Poland, Grand Duke of Finland
Alexander's Russia is a patient builder of the home front. His Builders do more, his Farms and Pastures grow productive, and every Governor brings Culture and Loyalty to the city they serve.

Alexander's bonuses reward a wide, well-governed empire. Builders get an extra [ICON_Charges] charge, Pastures yield more [ICON_Production] Production, and Farms grouped together add still more. Assign a [ICON_Governor] Governor to a city and the Zemstvo reform gives it [ICON_Culture] Culture and [ICON_PressureUp] Loyalty that grow with every era from the Medieval Era on, so even frontier cities stay stable. Upgrading units costs half as much [ICON_Gold] Gold, which keeps an old army modern without ruining the treasury. His agenda, The Liberator, makes other leaders like rulers who keep the peace and dislike those who recently declared war.

Alexander II (1818-1881) became Emperor of Russia in 1855, in the middle of the Crimean War. The defeat showed that the empire, vast but backward, could not keep its place in Europe without deep change. The reforms that followed earned him the name of the Tsar Liberator.

The greatest of them was the Manifesto of 19 February 1861, which freed more than twenty million peasants from serfdom. Freedom came with redemption payments and many limits, and the peasants were far from satisfied, but it opened the way to a new Russia.

The reforms that followed reshaped the state itself. In 1864 the zemstvos gave provinces and districts elected local self-government, and a new judicial system brought open courts and trial by jury. In 1874 the military reform of Dmitry Milyutin introduced universal conscription and modernized the army.

Abroad, Alexander ended the long Caucasian War in 1864 and pushed the borders of the empire into Central Asia, taking Tashkent and Samarkand. In 1867 he sold Russian America, Alaska, to the United States for 7.2 million dollars. The war with the Ottoman Empire in 1877-1878 freed Bulgaria, although the Congress of Berlin took back much of what Russia had won.

His reforms did not satisfy everyone. The Polish uprising of 1863 was crushed, and a growing revolutionary movement turned to terror. Alexander survived several attempts on his life. On 13 March 1881 (1 March in the old style) a bomb thrown by members of the People's Will fatally wounded him in Saint Petersburg, and the throne passed to his son Alexander III.
